passage: When archaeologists excavate a site, they record not only the objects they find but the exact layer and position in which each one lay. A pot is informative; a pot resting on a particular floor, beside a hearth, beneath a layer of ash, is far more so, because its surroundings fix it in time and link it to the activities around it. Objects that reach a museum stripped of this information—dug up by looters and sold without record—can still be admired, but much of what they could have told us is gone. This contrast suggests that, for archaeologists, the value of an excavated object depends heavily on ____
question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: the recorded context in which it was found, not on the object considered by itself.
whether the object is visually striking enough to merit display in a museum.
how many similar objects have already been recovered from other sites.
the speed with which it can be removed from the ground and conserved.

explanation: The correct answer is A. The passage contrasts an object whose layer and surroundings were recorded with one stripped of that information, and it says the second has lost much of what it could tell us, which points to context as the source of an object's value. A states that. B fastens on visual appeal, which the passage treats as separate from informational value; C introduces a count of similar finds the text never raises; and D emphasizes speed of removal, the opposite of the careful recording the passage praises.
